newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Volvo still positive to share buyback.
newsitem.headline: Volvo still positive to share buyback.

text.p: Swedish automotive group AB Volvo reiterated on Monday that it is in favour of Swedish authorities allowing companies to buy back their own shares.
"We are positive to companies having that possibility (to launch a share buyback plan)," Volvo spokesman Mats Edenborg told Reuters.
"Apart from the liquidity (Volvo) needs and necessary investments, it is good to have that possibility."
Edenborg said it would be up to Volvo's board whether the company did go ahead and buy back shares if the authorities gave permission for such a move.
Justice Ministry spokesman Sven Andersson said currently Swedish companies are very rarely allowed to buy back their own shares.
However the rules are under revision and a committee is expected to present a proposal in February.
"But if there was a new law, it would probably not take effect until January 1, 1999," Andersson said.
At Detroit's motor show last week, Volvo's chief executive officer Soren Gyll said cash in excess of a cushion of 15 percent of shareholders' funds would eventually be handed back to investors.
The 15 percent cushion would correspond to eight billion crowns ($1.2 billion) of Volvo's 15 billion crown cash pile, so the remaining part could be returned to investors.
But Edenborg downplayed the sum, saying Volvo also needed money for investments.

"Furthermore, there are other ways to return money to investors," said Per Lojdqvist, head of information at Volvo. "For example, we distributed (shares in tobacco subsidiary) Swedish Match to shareholders last year."
Analysts also shrugged off Volvo's interest in a share buyback.
"Volvo buying back shares is already partly in the share price," an analyst said.
Several cash-strong Swedish companies have expressed interest in a share buyback and analysts think it is a good idea in general.
With lower liquidity, the demand for return on equity would fall, giving the company a higher valuation, analysts said.
"There are many Swedish companies that would benefit from tidying their balance sheets," another analyst said.
-- Birgitta Forsberg, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1006 ($ = 6.887 Swedish Crowns)
